description:
Somos un equipo de ingenieros con experiencia en diseño de prototipos y un interés común: ayudar a los astronautas a cuidar su salud durante misiones de larga duración. 

Buscamos personas con habilidades en diseño de interfaces, visualización de datos, herramientas sin código o salud y fisiología. Si te motiva resolver un problema humano de la exploración espacial, te invitamos a diseñar con nosotros una herramienta sencilla de usar y a ponerla a prueba con casos simulados.
summary:
We developed ASTROCARE, a Python-based prototype that helps space crews assess their health and determine what to investigate when they notice a change. It operates offline, aggregating physical measurements, self-reported emotional states, results from reaction and memory mini-games, and environmental data.

The AI ​​module employs statistics and explainable, rule-based logic. It compares each health check against an individual’s personal history, identifies signs of stress or fatigue in voluntary comments, and looks for patterns across crew members sharing the same module. The interface displays which data points triggered an alert and suggests what should be examined. For instance, if two astronauts report a headache and miss more cues than usual, ASTRA correlates these inputs and suggests reviewing the cabin telemetry.

The dashboard visualizes trends and deviations, with an option to export data to Grafana. MoodHome allows crew members to manually adjust lighting and sound, then records how they feel afterward.

On missions with limited communication, ASTROCARE helps guide the response on board while maintaining a record for the medical team back on Earth. The demo integrates simulated health checks with historical radiation readings from NASA’s RadLab, tagged by date and the specific instrument used.
details:
ASTROCARE · Health monitor for space crews

What does it do and how does it work?

ASTROCARE is a prototype that helps the crew detect health changes and decide what to check while on board, even when communication with Earth is limited. It gathers biometric data, health self-assessments, results from reaction and memory mini-games, and environmental data. Its AI module operates locally, combining statistics with explainable rules. It compares measurements against each astronaut’s baseline, identifies patterns, and displays the specific data that triggered each alert.

One of its key contributions is the early monitoring of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). Using data from optical coherence tomography (OCT), intraocular pressure, and pupillometry, the app demonstrates how the monitor could flag persistent ocular changes and guide the crew on which measurements to review. Sleep and heart rate data provide additional context for the assessment. OCT has already been used on the International Space Station to evaluate the retina and the optic nerve. www.nasa.gov

ASTROCARE connects detection with action and follow-up. The advanced version features a smart Bluetooth-enabled patch containing liquid or gel-based medication in small, sealed reservoirs. Upon receiving a wireless command from a monitor, an internal mechanism, such as a micropump, releases a controlled amount through the skin. Continuous use of the patch allows for tracking trends between check-ups, distinguishing persistent changes from isolated spikes, and observing progress following an intervention. The patch is replaced once the reservoir is depleted or the adhesive reaches the end of its validated service life. The demo simulates the dispensing process and logs the medication, dosage, reason for administration, time, and remaining quantity.

We developed the prototype using Python, with JSON files for module data, a trends dashboard, and historical radiation readings from NASA’s RadLab. The design for local decision support draws inspiration from work at NASA Ames regarding medical operations with greater autonomy from Earth. www.nasa.gov

We took into account individual variability among astronauts, communication delays, potential sensor errors, and the need for clear alerts during high-stress situations. The prototype displays the signals that trigger each alert and maintains a reviewable history. Future implementation of autonomous dispensing would require the validation of sensors, medications, and dosages, as well as rigorous testing of system responses to connection losses or patch malfunctions.

It reduces the time between the initial onset of changes and their assessment on board. If a concerning trend is detected—for example, in ocular health—the crew can identify what has changed, when it began, and what specific parameters to monitor. Meanwhile, the medical team on Earth gains access to a comprehensive history, enabling them to reconstruct events, review the measures taken, and track the astronaut’s progress.

NASA already has tools in place to assess the cognitive and psychological health of its astronauts. Our proposal does not aim to replace these, but rather to explore a more interactive and accessible way to carry out such monitoring.

ASTRACARE combines cognitive games, emotional self-assessments, and trend visualization into a single, gamified experience.

Our goal is for well-being monitoring to be perceived not merely as a medical test, but as an activity integrated into an astronaut’s daily routine—one that makes it easier to observe their progress over time.

Furthermore, we designed this concept with the potential for adaptation to other environments characterized by isolation and stress.

We do more than just monitor the well-being of astronauts; we transform that monitoring into an interactive and engaging experience.
